newsitem.title: USA: Roycefield's antimony mine faces skeptics.
newsitem.headline: Roycefield's antimony mine faces skeptics.

text.p: Roycefield Resources' Beaver Brook antimony mine is due to start up in July and reach full capacity in the Fall, but some in the industry doubt if the company can meet its production plan.

Roycefield's Chief Financial Officer Paul Legere, said production would start in July and by September should reach full output of 5,000 tonnes a year of contained antimony in concentrates. All financing was in place, he said.
"Commercial antimony trioxide production will probably start in late 1998 or early 1999," Legere added. Until then the concentrates will be sold, although some may be tolled converted.
Beaver Brook is located near Gander in Newfoundland.
Some 80 percent of Western world demand is met by China. The minor metal is a key ingredient in flame retardant manufacturing.
Talks on sales contracts were almost finalised, with some concentrates left for spot deals, Legere said.
Roycefield at full output would account for 5 percent of current Western World demand of 100,000 tonnes a year, Legere said, who added that offtake was growing 5 to 6 percent a year.
Antimony prices have fallen in recent months, with the U.S. market stagnant at the moment, dealers said. Some doubted if Roycefield could produce what it has set out to do.
"I am not optimistic they can produce that much," Cyrus Malek of Oxxides Inc, an antimony trader, said.
Antimony metal prices have tumbled from $3,100 per tonne this time last year to $2,200 now, Malek said. "The market has got to bounce," Malek said.

Another dealer added: "The market is stagnant but I don't think there is any further weakness. We are hoping prices don't go any lower because they are at the point where producers cannot make any money and that's bad for the whole market."
Legere said:"We are very comfortable with the pricing as it is now. We feel we will be one of the lower cost producers." He declined to give any production costs at Beaver Brook.
But some traders wondered how Roycefield could make money by shipping concentrates abroad for conversion into trioxide at current prices.
Others said Roycefield may have problems finding buyers in the U.S. because of the level of sulfur in the concentrates.
Legere said some U.S. companies may be buyers of the concentrates which they would process outside the country.
He added that sulfur levels in the concentrates will be normal.
